PCI.BIO: Dr. Tarawneh is a Professor of Mechanical Engineering at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) where he worked since 2003. He obtained his MS and Ph.D. degrees from the University of Nebraska-Lincoln (UNL) in 1999 and 2003, respectively. He founded the University Transportation Center for Railway Safety (UTCRS) in 2013 and serves as the Founding Director. His various research and educational activities have resulted in $17.5 Million in funding from private industry, local, state, and federal sources. He has more than fourteen years of experience conducting a variety of railroad research with emphasis on advanced bearing condition monitoring techniques. He received 27 teaching, mentoring, and research awards highlighted by the UT System Regents’ Outstanding Teaching Award in 2009. To date he has taught 21 different courses in his discipline.

NCTEACH.AUDIENCE: External to The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
NCTEACH.ORG: University Transportation Center for Railway Safety (UTCRS)
NCTEACH.DESC: Supervised thirteen K-12 STEM teachers for five weeks through the UTCRS Research Experience for Teachers (RET) Program. Through this program, the selected teachers were mentored and trained on the use of transportation engineering STEM curricula in their specific disciplines and classes. The teachers were provided with ample hands-on engineering applications that can be brought to the classroom to engage and excite the young bright minds of tomorrow about STEM fields. Additionally, the teachers were introduced to the various ongoing projects and research activities associated with both, the University Transportation Center for Railway Safety (UTCRS) and the CREST Center for Multidisciplinary Research Excellence in Cyber-Physical Infrastructure Systems (MECIS), as a way of providing these teachers with avenues to bring some of these ideas back to their classrooms. Teachers acquired several skill-sets including programming, sensor technologies and functionalities, and hands-on training on developing engineering experimental setups and procedures.

NCTEACH.AUDIENCE: External to The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
NCTEACH.ORG: University Transportation Center for Railway Safety (UTCRS)
NCTEACH.DESC: Organized and offered a one-day workshop geared towards training K-12 STEM teachers on the use of the UTCRS developed STEM curricula (elementary, middle school, and high school). The curricula emphasizes STEM education using transportation engineering applications focused on railway safety. The workshop is interactive and teachers are engaged in hands-on activities related to the different educational modules. Teachers learn to program EV3 and MakeBlock mBot robots as part of the workshop activities. The workshop also features a challenge-based instruction session where teachers are mentored on how to apply these curricula in their classrooms and ways to utilize hands-on activities to make STEM learning more interesting and appealing to K-12 students. The teachers participating in the workshop must also present their ideas and plans to use what they learned in their classrooms as a requirement to get a certificate for this workshop.

NCTEACH.AUDIENCE: Internal to The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
NCTEACH.ORG: University Transportation Center for Railway Safety (UTCRS)
NCTEACH.DESC: A three-day workshop geared towards training the undergraduate and graduate student research assistants on the railroad research operations. The workshop included step-by-step procedures on proper instrumentation of the dynamic bearing test rigs and bearing condition monitoring techniques. The workshop also included a data analysis session utilizing Matlab to generate the temperature profiles, vibration signatures, dynamic and static load data, and axle rotation speed and power consumption. The students learned how to interpret this data and make decisions based on the results. This training is highly beneficial for any engineer that plans to work in a dynamic engineering environment.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Promoting Experiential Learning in STEM through Course-Based Undergraduate Research Experiences
Promoting Experiential Learning Through CUREs for Latinx Students
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Project Summary
The CUREs@RGV proposal is being submitted for consideration to the Engaged Student Learning Track (Track 1) as a design, development, and research study that will investigate the effects of a course-based undergraduate research experience (CURE) on undergraduate student outcomes, including learning, academic achievement, as well as attitudes and interest in STEM.
The first objective of this study is to provide professional development to STEM faculty (Biology, Biomedical, and Engineering) at UTRGV and STC to support their development and implementation of a CURE curriculum for undergraduate students. There is considerable evidence that CUREs improve student learning and interest in STEM. In addition, CUREs are an opportunity to provide more students with research experiences. The second objective of this study is to investigate faculty’s perceptions of undergraduate students’ abilities to engage in research and their self-efficacy toward designing and implementing CUREs. The third objective of this study will investigate the extent to which a CUREs laboratory affects (1) student learning outcomes and (2) attitudes/interest in STEM, as compared to learners experiencing a traditional lab. The fourth and final objective of this study is to strengthen the 2- to 4-year college pathway for STEM majors.
Intellectual Merit
To advance knowledge in STEM education and across STEM disciplines, we will draw from the literature on the development and implementation of CUREs (25, 47). Research demonstrates that CUREs improve students' achievement, retention, self-perceptions about learning, as well as scientific thinking and practices. The project team will support STEM faculty’s development of CUREs through a year-long professional development that includes development, implementation, and evaluation. The team will study the effects of CUREs curriculum on students’ learning, attitudes and interest in STEM. CUREs@RGV aims to 1) generate empirical evidence that will advance our understanding of how to improve undergraduate engagement, interest, and learning in STEM through CUREs; 2) improve STEM faculty’s self-efficacy toward CUREs and perceptions toward their students; and 3) strengthen pathways for students who have been marginalized in STEM education and careers. Because of the uniqueness of UTRGV, the study will focus on undergraduates who have been historically marginalized and underrepresented in STEM careers. This study draws on experiential learning theories and empirical findings in the literature on course-based undergraduate research experiences.
Broader Impacts
CUREs@RGV will lead to societal benefits in the short- and long-term. In the short-term, the project investigates ways to address the learning needs of undergraduate students in STEM courses through faculty professional development. The project will provide students, predominantly Latinx, with undergraduate research experiences that will lead to improved engagement, interest, and learning in STEM. The project will directly impact 24 STEM faculty at UTRGV and STC and approximately 600 undergraduate students in their CUREs course. In addition, over the three years, the project will indirectly impact 45 STEM faculty that attend the annual STEM Education conference, which is organized by the PI. A workshop will be conducted by the project team and in collaboration with the STEM faculty who have successfully implemented a CURE in their course. However, the ultimate impact is much broader as the research will be disseminated nationally through STEM education conference and journal publications. As a result, the project will help to broaden participation of Latinx students in STEM. The uniqueness of the RGV population is that more than 90% of the community is Latinx, of which approximately 85% are of Mexican descent.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Next Generation PTC-Integrated Onboard Smart Technologies and Training for Rolling Stock Condition Monitoring to Mitigate Train Derailment
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The Brotherhood of Railroad Signalmen (BRS) propose an initiative aimed at enhancing railway safety by proactively preventing train derailments caused by wheel and bearing  failure through the deployment of new onboard sensors, PTC connectivity and workforce training and deployment. BRS (in partnership with a technology provider, a university railway center and a railway testing facility) will research, plan, and implement a workforce development strategy to deploy this new technology as a supplement to the current wayside Hot Box Detectors (HBDs). The technology will provide the ability for carriers to identify and detect a potential failure well in advance of a catastrophic failure while railcars are in service. This project centers on the application of wireless onboard sensors, which measure temperature, vibration, and other metrics of railcar bearings and wheels, to the railroad industry environment to enhance the safety and efficacy of railroad operations. Implementation of this technology, and communications with the railroad, with real-time data, will dramatically increase the level of safety currently available and further reduce and/or eliminate the risk of a failure causing an on-road derailment while enhancing condition-based maintenance practices.

CONGRANT.TITLE: CREST Center for Multidisciplinary Research Excellence in Cyber-Physical Infrastructure Systems (MECIS)
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Overview:
The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) proposes to establish the “CREST Center for Multidisciplinary Research Excellence in Cyber-Physical Infrastructure Systems (MECIS).” The Center’s mission is to advance and transform the much-needed research and education at the nexus of automation, sensors, and artificial intelligence (AI), as integral parts of the “NSF’s 10 Big Ideas,” anticipating the revolutionary cyber-physical infrastructure systems (CIS). Three Colleges of Engineering, Sciences, and Education at UTRGV in collaboration with the Universities of Illinois (at Urbana-Champaign and at Chicago) and California (Riverside) will pursue multidisciplinary research on CIS, aiming to: (i) transfer technology to various transportation, logistics, manufacturing, and construction industries; and (ii) prepare a minority STEM workforce to drive future CIS-based communities. The Center envisions a portfolio of three research subprojects on automation, sensors, and AI that bridges diverse STEM disciplines. A holistic, multi-level approach is adopted to address CIS planning, design, and operation. While each subproject constitutes a unique element, their synergy ensures the CIS integrity.
Subproject 1 pushes the frontiers of knowledge in future transportation infrastructure, which will be transformed by autonomous vehicles (AVs) and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), in six directions: (i) at the planning level, public acceptance and policy issues of (U)AV; (ii-iv) at the design level, computer vision, automatic navigation, and model/field-based testing of the designed capabilities; and (v, vi) at the operation level, human-(U)AV interactions and network-wide inter-(U)AV interactions.
Subproject 2 designs and embeds sensors in CIS for two purposes. First, (U)AV sensors help perform automated tasks. Second, sensors in civil infrastructure and (U)AVs monitor infrastructure health. Three research areas are defined: (i, ii) at the design level, computational simulation, synthesis, and 3D printing of sensor materials and UAV structures, and (iii) at the operation level, cost-effective decision-making to upkeep infrastructure health using sensor data.
Since (U)AVs and sensors will inherently generate big data, Subproject 3 will synchronously work with subprojects 1 and 2 to: (i) develop AI solutions for big data management, and (ii) develop AI algorithms for big data analytics and decision making in the design and operation of (U)AVs and infrastructure.
UTRGV is the nation’s second largest Hispanic-Serving Institute (HIS) located in South Texas with an established record of preparing underrepresented minority students for STEM careers. The Center will provide (under)graduate students with cutting-edge CIS research experience, will integrate CIS research and education, and will pave a pathway from High School through graduate programs in STEM disciplines. This broad initiative at UTRGV will also offer new courses related to the subprojects. The Center will further enhance the research infrastructure at UTRGV and will strengthen the research competitiveness of a diverse group of faculty.
Intellectual Merit:
The proposed self-sustaining Center will play a key role in transforming the scientific discoveries at the intersection of automation, sensors, and AI technologies, which are the integral elements of next-generation CIS. The Center will address current gaps in the planning, design, and operation of CIS by proposing innovative theoretical, computational, experimental, and empirical solutions spanning from micro (molecule)- to macro (system)-scale, which also yield practical solutions valuable for the industry.
Broader Impacts:
The Center’s research and education activities will develop an underrepresented workforce equipped with the skills to address complex societal problems. The Center will partner with the public and private sectors to advance technology transfer and product development in CIS. The Center’s activities are key for the establishment of an inaugural engineering doctoral program, which will be vital in elevating UTRGV to a Research I institution and advancing the CIS research agenda in a predominantly HSI. The Center's research findings will be made available to the research community as journal publications and conference proceedings, which will inform other domains undergoing related transformations, such as the health industry, manufacturing and production systems, and the military.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Effect of Long-Term Inactivity on Railcar Bearing Lubricant Performance
CONGRANT.SPONORG: University Transfportation Center for Railway Safety
CONGRANT.AWARDORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The performance of railroad bearings that sit idle in railyards, large industrial plants, or shipping ports has only recently been explored. Some of the bearings, with documented periods of inactivity exceeding 18 months, have been associated with major derailments. This provides a basis for concerns that the inactive periods contributed to early failure, possibly through degradation of the grease properties brought on by moisture intake or grease separation leading to uneven protection of the metal components. The proposed work builds on prior efforts conducted in collaboration with CSX Transportation and seeks to improve our understanding of the effects of long-term inactivity on lubricant properties.

The proposed work would consist of (a) Preparation of test bearings which will be placed outdoors in a position to receive direct sunlight. (b) Placement of grease samples in the same location in a simulated bearing housing to mimic the thermal cycle of a sun-exposed bearing. (c) regular sampling from the simulated bearing housing to monitor long-term changes in lubricant performance and condition. (d) at intervals of 3 months, bearings will be removed and installed on a laboratory test rig and run for 1,000 simulated miles with continuous performance monitoring of temperature rise, vibration spectra, and power consumption, (e) post-test inspection including disassembly, teardown, and visual inspection of all bearing components, and (f) analysis of the grease composition at all stages with specific focus on loss of oxidation inhibitors and changes in tribological performance.

CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) is located in the historic Texan borderlands created at the end of the Mexican-American war in 1848 which separated families on both sides of the Rio Grande River. The university was formed in 2013 when The University of Texas at Brownsville and The University of Texas Pan-American were consolidated to expand educational opportunities in the underserved and rural Valley of the Rio Grande. UTRGV is a major Hispanic-Serving Institution (HSI), primarily a nonresidential, 4-year, public, R2 institution, with campuses situated along the lower 100 miles of the Rio Grande. UTRGV's student demographics mirror those of the Lower Rio Grande Valley (RGV), with over 95% of our 32,000 students being of Hispanic or Latinx origin (Region One Education Service Center, 2021), and over 85% having Mexican-American heritage. Academic programs in engineering, started in 1992, were first accredited by ABET in 1996. The College of Engineering and Computer Science (CECS) currently has 6 departments offering 8 bachelors' and 7 masters' degrees. The college has over 110 faculty members and serves nearly 3900 students, mostly (90%) undergraduates. Although CECS does not have a PhD program yet, a pathway for a doctoral degree is offered jointly with the University of Nebraska at Lincoln (UNL). As the second largest HSI in the nation, UTR V is uniquely positioned to broaden the participation of Hispanics in the engineering workforce.
CONGRANT.OTHER_AGENCIES: The proposal focuses on increasing “effective STEM education and broadening participation” in underrepresented minority STEM students at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) to successfully face academic and professional challenges, recently exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic. The Freshman Year Innovator Experience proposes the development of self-transformation skills in freshman mechanical engineering students to successfully face academic and professional challenges exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic while working on two parallel projects of technical design innovation and academic career pathways.

Effect of Climate-induced Extreme Temperature on Rail Network Safety
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Temperature is one of the major factors related to the buckling of railway tracks. Due to the increase in frequency and intensity of heat waves in recent years, there is a need to study the effect of climate-induced extreme temperature events on the vulnerability of the rail infrastructure to buckling. CONGRANT.TITLE: Strategies and Technologies for Warning, Detection, and Prevention of Trespassing in the Vicinity of Highway-Rail Grade Crossings: State of the Practice and Research Needs
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The U.S. rail network is the largest, safest, and most efficient rail network in the world that operates over 160,000 rail miles. It plays a pivotal role in enabling the transportation of goods and people throughout the nation; and due to this crucial function, it serves as a fundamental pillar in supporting the economic expansion of the United States (Federal Railroad Administration, 2023). Simultaneously, the U.S. highway network plays a crucial role in enabling the seamless transportation of both individuals and cargo, consisting of a sophisticated linked grid of roads that spans the entire nation. According to data from the U.S. Department of Transportation (USDOT), the average monthly traffic volume for the year 2022 exceeded 3,000 billion miles. However, at the intersection of these two crucial transportation modes lies a point of concern—the Highway Rail Grade Crossing (HRGC).
HRGCs are where a road or pathway intersects with a railway track. These crossings facilitate the safe passage of vehicles, cyclists, and pedestrians across railway lines. However, if road users fail to notice warning signals and attempt to cross the tracks when a train is approaching, a catastrophic collision can occur, leading to severe injuries or fatalities. As such, HRGCs are a critical cause of hazardous conditions that may involve collisions between trains and vehicles or pedestrians. Thousands of highway-rail incidents occur in the US every year. Such incidents include many fatal crashes. Between 2010 and 2018, a total of 1,114 fatal crashes tragically occurred at HRGCs in the United States that resulted in the loss of 1,306 lives.
Trespassing at-or-near HRGC is a major safety issue. Trespassers are most often pedestrians trying to take a shortcut and/or do not notice incoming trains. Although it is illegal, more than 400 rail trespass fatalities occur every year. Various technologies and practices have been proposed to detect trespassing at rail crossings. Such technologies can involve various types of sensors such as radar, laser, infrared, magnetic, and many others. Such technologies can be infrastructure-based, locomotive-based, or a combination of both. Some innovative technologies include CCTV cameras assisted by computer vision, depth-sensing cameras, stereo vision, laser systems, and smart sensors enabled by deep learning, among others. Naturally, various technologies and practices come with diverse considerations, including aspects like their reliability, cost-effectiveness, accuracy, and smooth integration into rail infrastructure systems. There is a need to explore the advantages and disadvantages of existing and emerging technologies considering the needs and challenges of the rail infrastructure. The outcomes of this exploratory investigation guide decision-making and future research to prevent trespassing at HRGCs and improve the safety of the U.S. rail network.

CONGRANT.SPONORG: U.S. Department of Transportation (USDOT) UTC Program
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
This proposal establishes the Center for Integrated Transportation Infrastructure 4.0 (CITI-4.0), a National University Transportation Center focusing on “Improving the Durability and Extending the Life of Transportation Infrastructure”. CITI 4.0 is a consortium of seven US higher education and research institutions that consolidate their expertise, facilities, resources, and institutional support to achieve the common goals of the center. The center addresses the challenges of the new era Intelligent Transportation System in ways never previously imagined by adapting the “Industry 4.0” principles to the integrated transportation infrastructure. CITI-4.0 introduces automation, cyber-physical fusion and information driven practices, enabled by real-time data communications among heterogeneous monitoring sensors and integrates the assessment, management and maintenance activities of the infrastructure, resources and operations across railways, roadways, and ports following a data-driven performance-based approach.

Motives: North America’s demand for safe, affordable, and environmentally responsible transportation of people and goods by railway, roadway, and ports is projected to grow substantially in the years ahead. Asset managers are consistently challenged to improve the performance of the transportation network, optimize efficiency of operations and ensure safety by maximizing accessibility and reliability of the transportation infrastructure. Although accurate monitoring is a key enabler for effective operations and maintenance, the condition assessment is currently conducted based mainly on periodic, labor-intensive and time-consuming scheduled activities. The interpretation of the collected data and integration with operations is extensively dependent on the experience of the operators and other human factors. Each transportation mode relies typically on its own operations, infrastructure, and resources to meet the current network demand. These three elements are often loosely integrated within each mode, are rarely integrated across modes, and are not effectively engaged with the end users of the network.

Topic Areas: The center activities cover the following non-exclusive topics: (1) Application of new materials and technologies; (2) Cyber and communications security; (3) Condition monitoring, remote sensing, and the use of GPS; (4) Asset and performance management through data accessibility, data security and analytical tools;

Impacts: CITI-4.0 brings the infrastructure of the major transportation modes into the Industry 4.0 era as essential parts of the grand Intelligent Transportation System. The proposed CITI-4.0 research, education, workforce development, technology transfer, and diversity activities advance technology in transportation engineering and enable students and professionals from diverse socioeconomic groups throughout the country to develop the skills necessary to overcome the transportation challenges of the next era and create the next generation of worldwide leaders. This initiative benefits all stakeholders in the transportation industry, administration and legislation and sets the framework for addressing similar problems around the world.

CONGRANT.TITLE: IntelligentSelf-Powered Wireless Sensing (ISPWS) System for Onboard Real-time Health Monitoring and Proactive Damage Detection of Freight Trains
CONGRANT.SPONORG: The National Academies of Sciences Engineering Medicine
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Ensuring the safety of the freight railway network is essential for enabling the safe, reliable, and efficient movement of goods in the United States. Freight railcars are susceptible to wheel misalignment due to excessive speeding on curves, track defects, and failures of the critical components of their suspension systems that is usually caused by hunting oscillation, overheating, and impact. The current practice for condition monitoring of the critical components of freight railcars, such as wheel bearings, relies on trackside methods which are based on the deployment of sensors on the track in isolated locations. These methods are inherently “reactive,” implying that they resort to an unappealing find-and-fix strategy which act only when the target component is already damaged. In addition, they require a large amount of external power which makes them costly.

The objective of this research proposal is to develop the proof-of-concept prototype of an onboard self-powered wireless sensing system for real-time health monitoring and prediction of the wheel bearings of freight railcars by employing a “proactive” damage detection strategy developed based on online machine learning. The wireless sensing system is battery-less and is powered by an onboard electromagnetic energy harvester with a high-power density.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Prototyping and Testing of Electrically Conductive Thermoplastic Poyurethane Railroad Suspension Pad
CONGRANT.SPONORG: University Transportation Center for Railroad Safety
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: This research will take formulations of carbon nanofibers in thermoplastic polyurethanes (TPU), which have shown promising levels of electric conductivity, for use in a conductive steering pad, and prepare them for deployment in a commercially viable product. Plain elastomers are insulators and prevent transmission of current from rail to frame to signal door or gate opening devices. In addition, the thermal insulating properties of these materials reduce the rate of heat flow from bearings through the bearing adapter and into the side-frame, where it can be dissipated. Previous studies performed by the University Transportation Center for Railway Safety (UTCRS) revealed that traditional conductive additives, such as carbon black, must be applied at high volume fraction in order to generate sufficient conductivity, which in turn results in substantial increases in pad stiffness and degradation of pad durability.  Vapor Grown Carbon Nanofibers (VGCNF) are extremely efficient conductive additives that can produce the desired conductivity at much lower concentrations and with less impact on mechanical performance than traditional additives. Prior efforts have identified a TPU carbon nanofiber combination and fiber loading that produces excellent conductivity, and results in an electrically conductive part when molded under commercially useful molding temperatures. The identified system first needs to be scaled from laboratory quantity testing to injection molding quantities, and then prototyped. Moreover, the microstructural contributions to conductivity as well as the allowable processing range need to be fully described in order to support process development and quality control processes in commercialization.

Objective #2 – Create and Implement the Cross-Sector Partnerships Leadership Institute that establishes projects that develop mutually beneficial partnerships to build faculty capacity and student opportunities to conduct STEM research or STEM education research at HSIs. Project services will include NSF Proposal writing and financial compliance training, in addition to facilitating networking and professional development opportunities that build and strengthen collaborations among HSIs.  
Objective #3 – Create and Implement the Research on Broadening Participation in STEM Leadership Institute that will generate new knowledge about how to enhance undergraduate STEM education that results in an increase in retention and graduation rates of undergraduate students pursuing degrees in STEM fields at HSIs.

Ultimately, the success of this project will produce a more qualified, innovative, and diverse STEM workforce. Overview: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) and its University Transportation Center for Railway Safety (UTCRS) aim to establish a new Engineering RET Site entitled: “Transportation Engineering Research in STEM Fields.” Since transportation engineering is an interdisciplinary field, the teachers will be exposed to research projects from mechanical, electrical, civil, and manufacturing and industrial engineering disciplines. STC is the largest Hispanic serving community college in the nation with over 34,000 students, of whom 70% are first generation college goers, over 95% are Hispanic, and greater than 75% are on financial aid. La Joya ISD is the fourth largest school district in the Lower Rio Grande Valley and home to 30,000 PreK-12 students (99.7% Hispanic) and 2,035 teachers. Both La Joya ISD and PSJA ISD are among the highest poverty rates in the U.S. Ten STEM teachers and faculty will be recruited annually from STC, PSJA ISD, and La Joya ISD to participate in the proposed RET program. The teachers/faculty will spend ten weeks per year as part of their involvement in the RET Program. Six of the ten weeks will be spent on the UTRGV campus during the summer, and the remaining four weeks will be effort expended during the academic year developing and implementing modules and interactive hands-on activities in STEM classrooms, and presentations to other teachers in organized STEM teacher workshops and symposiums. Constantine Tarawneh, Principal Investigator, Ph. (956) 867-5907, constantine.tarawneh@utrgv.edu, will serve as the point-of-contact for teacher/faculty recruitment. The RET Site will utilize the existing UTCRS web site http://railwaysafety.utrgv.edu/. 
Key Words: transportation engineering research, railway safety, bearing condition monitoring, advanced sensor technologies, STEM teacher workshops and symposiums, STEM teaching modules.   
2.	Intellectual Merit: The proposed UTRGV RET Site is different from any of the previously NSF funded sites in that it focuses on transportation engineering research as an interdisciplinary field of study encompassing mechanical, electrical, civil, and manufacturing and industrial engineering. There has been only one transportation related site previously funded through NSF entitled: “Innovative Transportation Systems,” which focused on transportation solutions in rural areas. The new proposed RET Site will introduce faculty and teachers to a broad range of transportation engineering research in areas such as advanced bearing condition monitoring techniques, proactive maintenance cycles for railroad rolling stock, advanced sensor technologies, advanced materials research, and intelligent control systems. The teachers/faculty will be seamlessly integrated with the ongoing research teams and will work on preparing grade-level appropriate teaching and research modules that the faculty/teachers can implement in their respective STEM classrooms. 3. As current leaders in the transportation industry near retirement, it is imperative that we cultivate the next generation of highly-skilled workforce that will deliver our twenty-first century transportation infrastructure. The proposed RET Site aims at working hand-in-hand with our teachers/faculty to bring transportation engineering into K-16 classrooms with the purpose of  motivating and exciting historically underrepresented students to pursue careers in this interdisciplinary field to meet the needs of the aging transportation workforce.

CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Researchers at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) have developed patent pending technologies to convert waste glass into single-digit micron and sub-micron (300±200 nanometers) glass particles that have unique properties not found in bulk glass. Waste glass is typical soda lime glass with about 60-90% silica and 40-10% other (sodium, calcium, and aluminum) oxides. The principal investigators (PIs) at UTRGV have found that the properties of recycled glass fine particles that have been processed into superfine particles are dramatically different. The PIs are interested in understanding the myriad of processing-property-microstructure relationships of these glass particles and composites (i.e., multi-layer fabric reinforced with shear thickening fluids made from these particles). The basic science research component of this DoD project will initially concentrate on submicron silica or glass particles by themselves to define and demonstrate systematically the underlying processing-property-microstructure relationships, and their controlled manipulation under dynamic conditions to create the next generation composites for superior performance. Modeling efforts will include experimentally informed and validated finite element analysis. After gaining a thorough insight into each type of particle, the study will be extended to the combination of micron and submicron silica and glass particles. The soda-lime glass fine particles can be commercially produced from waste glass for under a dollar (target price) a pound, which also has a positive impact on the environment through recycling. Equally relevant is the fact that it is foreseen that these submicron glass particles can be produced in commercial quantities of tens of tons per day. These new materials and derived material systems and their properties have a great potential to address key Department of Defense, ARMY Research Office (ARO) interests. Specifically, (a) detailed understanding of complex material system behavior and its capability during service, and (b) to utilize material’s capabilities close to their limiting capacity (ARO, Solid Mechanics - Understanding of Mechanical Behavior of Complex Material Systems). In order to further motivate, inspire, and engage STEM students at UTRGV, additional educational/outreach activities will include a number of focused DoD applied research projects that are linked with the basic science research, which will attract and actively engage undergraduate senior design groups. Relating to the ARO Mechanical Behavior of Materials, the aim of body armor applied research is to develop a low cost, lightweight, wearable garment system with ballistic impact resistance which is very amenable to our basic research. In addition, all research/educational results will be published in journals and conferences and presented to the rest of the student body at UTRGV at professional symposiums and poster presentations highlighting DoD opportunities for student professional development. It is important to note that the PIs have all the necessary facilities and equipment (including a new state-of-the-art oven with programmable and controlled environment including vacuum and inert gases) to perform the proposed basic and applied research. Some of the equipment has been designed and fabricated here at UTRGV by our undergraduate students under the supervision of the PIs.

CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The proposed US DOT University Transportation Center for Railway Safety (UTCRS) will deploy research teams focused on improving the durability and extending the life of railway transportation systems within the United States. Informed by state-of-the-art safety data reporting and management paradigms, the UTCRS teams will concentrate their research efforts in the following areas:

• Improving durability and extending the life of safety-critical components of rolling stock, including draw-gear, axles, wheels, and bearings;
• Increasing durability and extending the life of rail with a focus on reducing the potential for broken rail under service;
• Improving durability and extending the life of rail support systems, including cross tie systems, ballast systems, and base and sub-base foundational systems;
• Increasing durability and extending the life of railway bridge structures via an integrated systems approach to modeling, design, construction, inspection, and maintenance that includes strategic cyber-infrastructure systems technology development and deployment;
• Investigate and develop strategic engineered system asset and performance management technologies;
• Investigate and develop railway construction process methodologies and railway construction and maintenance management systems that lead to improved product outcomes in terms of durability and fault-free service life; and
• Identify and investigate technology that increases opportunities for railway transportation to increase the durability, life, and safety of highway transportation through strategic shifting of freight haul services.

Aging Infrastructure: An Integrated Systems Approach to Improving Railway Transportation Systems
It is increasingly understood that the disparate physical aspects of railway transportation systems cannot be treated separately, but must in reality be modeled, designed, inspected, and maintained as integrated systems and systems of systems. Each asset and its constituent components can and does affect the performance of interfacing assets and their components. For example, the rails interact in a very complex manner with the wheels, bearings, and axles of the rolling stock. Furthermore, the rails interact with the track structure foundational elements (ties, ballast, base and sub-base) in a very complex and time-, temperature-, moisture-, and load-dependent and evolutionary manner over the life of the railway. Unfortunately, it has not been customary in the past to treat these interfaced components as integrated systems. Guided by cutting-edge systems-of-systems research principles, the UTCRS research teams will directly address the co-dependencies and mutual dependencies within and among the assets upon which safe and reliable railway transportation depends.

CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
This project will develop multimodal Engineering Mechanics modules (i.e. incorporating multiple
modes of physical or virtual interaction) designed to teach concepts through experimentation to
students with limited Calculus and Physics proficiency. The modules will serve three audiences:
1. Undergraduate engineering majors who struggle to conceptualize Engineering Mechanics,
2. Non-engineering undergraduates seeking a technical minor or associates degree,1 and
3. High-school students learning basic Mechanics in Mathematics and Science courses.
Students struggle to conceptualize Engineering Mechanics (i.e. Newtonian Physics, Statics,
and Dynamics) fundamentals because they cannot effectively visualize the effects of external
loads on physical systems and/or do not intuitively comprehend the static or dynamic response
[1]. Traditionally, Engineering Mechanics courses have been primarily lecture-based with little
experimentation. The PIs contend that through the use of simple bench-top experiments or virtual
representations of physical systems, students, especially those who underperform or show limited
proficiency in Calculus and Physics, can more effectively interpret concepts. Furthermore, such
tools are more effective at overcoming common misconceptions.
INTELLECTUAL MERIT: The multimodal modules will be designed to encourage properly conceived
understanding of fundamentals through discovery and experience to better address common
misconceptions. The modules will engender proper engineering intuition and critical thinking by
forcing students to discover and identify the underlying principles. The focus will be more on facilitating
development of qualitative analysis and less on quantitative problem solving skills. This
project will formally and exhaustively assess the impact of using multimodal curriculum to (1)
dispel common Engineering Mechanics misconceptions and (2) enable students with limited proficiency
in the underlying Mathematics and Physics. The multimodal modules will be based, in part,
on modules previously developed and piloted at The University of Texas-Pan American (UTPA)
with the support of seed money from the Mechanical Engineering Department.
BROADER IMPACT: The modules will also be tested at the South Texas College (STC), a regional
community college, and at South Texas Independent School District’s Business, Education,
and Technology Academy (b ETA), a local school serving grades 7-12. At UTPA the modules
will be used for engineering majors, technology related minors, and K-12 students participating in
summer programs. The modules will be organized into a comprehensive series that will be readily
scalable to the various target audiences. Successful development, implementation, and evaluation
will enable widespread use of such modules at other institutions and in other disciplines.
Less than 10%of entering freshman at UTPA begin their Math sequence in Calculus I or higher.
This generates a significant delay till students are eligible to take entry level Engineering courses
or even prerequisites, which threatens the retention of first-year Engineering students. To combat
this, an Introduction to Engineering course with no Math or Physics prerequisites is offered to
all students and is a first-year requirement for Engineering majors. Using multimodal modules
in early courses such as this and throughout the Engineering Mechanics sequence will preempt
misconceptions and reinforce properly founded understanding. The modules can replace specific
homework assignments or lectures.

Drawing on the community wealth asset framework, the CBPE -E3 is grounded in culturally relevant programming and pedagogy. The CBPE -E3 expands University X's student educational opportunities through an R1 institution collaboration to create the Alliance for Student Participation in Research Experiences for Hispanics (ASPIRE Hispanics). Finally, the CBPE -E3 shares promising practices with institutions serving largely Hispanic populations so that they can replicate or adapt best practices at their home campuses through an "Equity in Engineering Education Summit." INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: A thermoelectric energy harvesting device is evaluated to power a bearing health monitoring system. Contrary to wayside equipment, the new system is an onboard wireless solution utilizing accelerometer and temperature sensors to assess the bearing condition continuously. The harvesting system consists of two thermoelectric generator modules with aluminum heat sinks, a switching boost converter, a battery management circuit, and a lithium rechargeable battery. The performance of the harvester is validated on an AAR class bearing mounted on a laboratory tester, with load and speed simulating common freight routes of up to 896 miles. The energy harvested varies with load, speed, and bearing condition. However, over a realistic route, the net energy harvested is more than double that consumed by the sensor, indicating that the operating life without maintenance will be limited by component life rather than battery capacity. The critical design parameters are the ratio of open circuit voltage to temperature difference for the thermoelectric module, and the cold start voltage of the boost converter.

INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT:
Many freight railcars rest on polymer adapter pads made of injection-molded Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU) polymers which feature two copper studs to provide electrical conductivity through the pad. This design feature allows signal transmission from the track to the onboard systems, including cargo gates and pneumatic actuators. While in service, the polymer pads experience impact and cyclic loading that produce shear, resulting in the abrasive wear and plastic compression of the copper studs which leads to signal interruptions and loss of function requiring the periodic replacement of these polymer pads. This causes increased downtime due to maintenance and reduced reliability in the automated systems since pad failure is unpredictable. This limitation in current designs is the driving concern behind the effort to create an electrically conductive polymer adapter pad that would provide a durable conductive path between the rail and freight car side-frame.

To that end, the University Transportation Center for Railway Safety (UTCRS) has been working on developing a conductive composite blend of TPU and Carbon Nano Fibers (CNF) to create injection-molded polymer composite inserts that can provide the necessary conductivity without the need for the copper studs that are susceptible to wear. Previous work done on this project was successful in creating a TPU-CNF composite insert that provided the required electrical conductivity at full railcar loads but was inconsistent at empty railcar loads. Thus, current work presented here focused on studying the fiber orientation that would produce consistent conductivity at all railcar loads. Based on these findings, a new mold was fabricated to create injection-molded polymer composite inserts with the effective fiber orientation. Laboratory test results show that the newly created composite inserts provide approximately double the needed conductivity required for a 24-Volt railcar valve to actuate when tested under the minimum load conditions an adapter would experience in field service. This paper summarizes the work done on fiber alignment and the results of the testing performed on the UTCRS dynamic bearing test rigs.

INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Researchers at the University Transportation Center for Railway Safety (UTCRS) have developed an onboard wireless monitoring device to gauge the health of freight railcar rolling stock. A wireless system will allow for preemptive maintenance to occur, potentially saving millions of dollars in damages and ensuring the safety of passengers and cargo. A prototype energy harvester has been developed that can extend the battery life of the wireless monitoring device. It uses Thermoelectric Generators (TEGs) mounted on the bearing adapter to convert heat generated from the bearings to electricity. Previous results have shown that, under optimal conditions, TEGs have been able to produce enough energy to meet the power demands of low-power circuit boards. This paper summarizes the proof-of-concept validation of the complete energy harvesting device which includes the performance of the TEGs, heat sinks, boost converter, and the Battery Management Chip (BMC) working in tandem. The testing results were acquired by replicating field service conditions using a test plan that reproduces speeds encountered on a realistic railroad route and run on a laboratory dynamic bearing test rig. The test plan simulates a train completing a round trip between Billings, MT and Council Bluffs, IA. Preliminary testing results show that, over an average trip where train speeds vary, the energy harvesting system can significantly extend the battery life by producing enough energy to maintain or increase the charge of the battery while also powering the sensors and wireless transceiver for the duration of the trip.

INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT:
The “internet of things” has revolutionized the methods in which many industries have optimized performance and component defect detection by providing real-time feedback through the implementation of data processing and wireless communication. Despite these advancements, the railway industry has lingered stagnant in its approach of adopting these advanced prognostic detection systems, and instead relies on discretely (25–40 miles) placed trackside condition monitoring systems, aka wayside. These wayside systems are primarily used to detect abnormal operating conditions in railcar rolling stock components. However, while they have been used for decades to address imminent threats to derailments and/or safety, they have unfortunately been shown to erroneously flag and misdiagnose components. These “false positive” cases usually result in unnecessary and costly delays and train stoppages. In worst case scenarios, these wayside systems have been known to mis-identify problematic components which can potentially lead to catastrophic derailments, risking property and safety. Overall, these limitations to established methods, and current technological innovations, allow for the introduction of a pioneering technology that addresses these deficiencies to enable constant, reliable, and precise onboard component health monitoring through vibration and temperature tracking. With these advancements, railroad car owners and operators can preemptively assess any rolling stock maintenance issue well in advance of an anticipated catastrophic failure.

To validate the efficacy of these onboard sensors, a field study was conducted using 40 such monitoring devices that were affixed to the bearing adapters of randomly selected railcars in a dedicated coal service route. After the span of two months of ongoing testing, three wheelsets were selected for removal based on data collected that indicated non-normative operating conditions. The wheelsets were inspected, analyzed, and the corresponding bearings were shipped to the University Transportation Center for Railway Safety (UTCRS) for laboratory evaluation and testing. This paper summarizes some of the preliminary results acquired from this field test and provides a comparison between the field and laboratory data, demonstrating their agreement and the prospective integration of these sensor technologies into the rail industry.

INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT:
Bearing temperature serves as an important metric used in identifying defective bearings in the rail industry. Current defect detection systems, such as the Hot Box Detectors (HBDs), are used to measure the temperature of freight car roller bearings. The HBD is a wayside device that utilizes a non-contact infrared sensor to determine the operating temperature of a railroad bearing as it passes over the HBD. Railroads analyze the data collected by HBDs to detect and flag defective bearings. If the operating temperature of a bearing surpasses a predetermined threshold, an emergency stop is initiated, and the bearing is removed from service and sent for inspection. One major drawback of HBDs is that they have been associated with many “false positives,” which has resulted in costly train stoppages and delays.

To combat that, researchers have opted to use wireless onboard sensor devices mounted directly on the bearing adapter. One such device is the wireless onboard health monitoring system developed by the University Transportation Center for Railway Safety (UTCRS) that utilizes temperature and vibration sensors to detect the condition of rolling stock. However, because the device is affixed to the bearing adapter and not the bearing itself, the strategic placement of the temperature sensor on the adapter is crucial in minimizing the thermal lag associated with the heat transfer from the bearing to the location where the temperature is measured, as this will directly affect the accuracy of the readings. By conducting a transient heat transfer finite element analysis (FEA), the estimated time-lag and the temperature distribution within the bearing adapter can be determined. To validate the accuracy of the transient FEA model, the results were compared to data acquired from laboratory testing performed on the UTCRS dynamic bearing test rigs. The results obtained in this study can be used to identify optimal anchor points for the temperature sensors on the bearing adapter, and in turn, increase the proficiency of wireless onboard sensor devices in detecting defective components.

INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT:
Rail transportation plays an important role in today’s economy by delivering a large quantity of goods and passengers to various locations throughout North America in an economic and efficient manner. Bearing failure is one of the leading causes of derailments that result in significant capital loss and in extreme cases tragic human loss. The two widely used bearing health monitoring systems are the Trackside Acoustic Detection System (TADS™) and the wayside Hot-Box Detector (HBD). These systems are reactive in nature and only give alerts when the bearings are nearing failure. To supplant that, a prototype wireless onboard condition monitoring system was developed by researchers at the University Transportation Center for Railway Safety (UTCRS). This onboard wireless system can detect bearing defects at their early stages of initiation so that proactive maintenance actions can be taken by the railroads and railcar owners. Due to the wireless nature of this system, a constant power supply is needed to ensure its continued operation.

Currently, the prototype wireless system utilizes low-power circuitry that is powered by a rechargeable AA battery that can provide up to two years of operation depending on usage. Implementation of a suitable energy harvesting device can significantly increase the longevity of the batteries used in the wireless module, and in ideal operating conditions, generate consistent energy rendering the battery as a temporary energy storage device. The proposed energy harvesting device consists of thermoelectric generators, aluminum heat sinks, a switching boost convertor, and a battery management chip. This device was tested on a dynamic bearing test rig to assess the performance of the thermoelectric generators. To best simulate field operation conditions, the thermoelectric generators were placed on opposite sides of the bearing adapter; one exposed to direct forced convection while the other side is shielded by the adapter and experiences minimal convection. Thermoelectric generators were found to be an effective solution due to their ability to convert a temperature gradient into a usable voltage sufficient to charge the battery. The buck booster converter increases the voltage from the thermoelectric generators to 5-volts so that the battery management chip can regulate the voltage and efficiently charge the battery. This paper summarizes the performance of the thermoelectric modules under different operating conditions. The main goal of this project is to devise an energy harvesting device that allows the wireless module to be self-powered utilizing the heat generated from the bearing and the charge held by the battery as a hybrid power source.

INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Currently, there are two types of defect detection systems used to monitor the health of freight railcar bearings in service: wayside hot-box detection (HBD) systems and trackside acoustic detection (TAD) systems. These systems have proven to be inefficient in accurately determining bearing health, especially in the early stages of defect detection. To that end, a prototype onboard bearing condition monitoring system has been developed and validated through extensive laboratory testing and a designated field test in 2015 at the Transportation Technology Center Inc (TTCI) in Pueblo, CO. INTELLCONT.TITLE: Nothing is Impossible: Characteristics of Persistent Hispanic Females in STEM
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Factors that influence the underrepresentation of females in STEM careers begin early in childhood when gender biases and stereotypes emerge. Stereotypes have a psychosocial effect on females that can lead to low self-efficacy and less interest in learning and pursuing STEM careers. This study investigated the effect of a STEM summer camp onK-12 students learning in which upper elementary students explored STEM concepts through magnetic levitation (MagLev) train activities, middle school students built and programmed robots, and high school students explored STEM through both MagLev train and robotics activities. A mixed methods design was used to analyze pre/posttest scores of all students and interviews of randomly selected Hispanic female students. Data indicated that Hispanic, high school females were less likely to participate in the STEM summer camp as compared to their elementary or middle school counterparts. In addition, there were no gender differences in academic achievement at the elementary level, but Hispanic females reported significantly higher learning gains than Hispanic males. In high school, Hispanic females reported significantly lower pretest scores than males. We conclude that there is a change in the characteristics, attitudes, and academic achievement of Hispanic females from elementary to high school, but informal STEM opportunities can mitigate this change.

INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT:
There are currently two primary wayside detection systems for monitoring the health of freight railcar bearings in the railroad industry: The Trackside Acoustic Detection System (TADS™) and the wayside Hot-Box Detector (HBD). TADS™ uses wayside microphones to detect and alert the train operator of high-risk defects. However, many defective bearings may never be detected by TADS™ since a high-risk defect is a spall which spans about 90% of a bearing’s raceway, and there are less than 30 systems in operation throughout the United States and Canada. HBDs sit on the side of the rail-tracks and use non-contact infrared sensors to acquire temperatures of bearings as they roll over the detector. These wayside bearing detection systems are reactive in nature and often require emergency stops in order to replace the wheelset containing the identified defective bearing. Train stoppages are inefficient and can be very costly. Unnecessary train stoppages can be avoided if a proper maintenance schedule can be developed at the onset of a defect initiating within the bearing. Using a proactive approach, railcars with defective bearings could be allowed to remain in service operation safely until reaching scheduled maintenance.
The University Transportation Center for Railway Safety (UTCRS) research group at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) has been working on developing a proactive bearing condition monitoring system which can reliably detect the onset of bearing failure. Unlike wayside detection systems, the onboard condition monitoring system can continuously assess the railcar bearing health and can provide accurate temperature and vibration profiles to alert of defect initiation. This system has been validated through rigorous laboratory testing at UTRGV and field testing at the Transportation Technology Center, Inc. (TTCI) in Pueblo, CO. The work presented here builds on previously published work that demonstrates the use of the onboard condition monitoring system to identify defective bearings as well as the correlations developed for spall growth rates of defective bearing outer rings (cups). The system first uses the root-mean-square (RMS) value of the bearing’s acceleration to assess its health. Then, an analysis of the frequency domain of the acquired vibration signature determines if the bearing has a defective inner ring (cone) and the RMS value is used to estimate the defect size. This estimated size is then used to predict the residual life of the bearing. The methodology proposed in this paper can assist railroads and railcar owners in the development of a proactive and cost-efficient maintenance cycle for their rolling stock.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Optimization of Railroad Bearing Health Monitoring System for Wireless Utilization

INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT:
In the railroad industry, systematic health inspections of freight railcar bearings are required. Bearings are subjected to high loads and run at high speeds, so over time the bearings may develop a defect that can potentially cause a derailment if left in service operation. Current bearing condition monitoring systems include Hot-Box Detectors (HBDs) and Trackside Acoustic Detection Systems (TADS™). The commonly used HBDs use non-contact infrared sensors to detect abnormal temperatures of bearings as they pass over the detector. Bearing temperatures that are about 94°C above ambient conditions will trigger an alarm indicating that the bearing must be removed from field service and inspected for defects. However, HBDs can be inconsistent, where 138 severely defective bearings from 2010 to 2019 were not detected. And from 2001 to 2007, Amsted Rail concluded that about 40% of presumably defective bearings detected by HBDs did not have any significant defects upon teardown and inspection. TADS™ use microphones to detect high-risk bearings by listening to their acoustic sound vibrations. Still, TADS™ are not very reliable since there are less than 30 active systems in the U.S. and Canada, and derailments may occur before bearings encounter any of these systems.
Researchers from the University Transportation Center for Railway Safety (UTCRS) have developed an advanced algorithm that can accurately and reliably monitor the condition of the bearings via temperature and vibration measurements. This algorithm uses the vibration measurements collected from accelerometers on the bearing adapters to determine if there is a defect, where the defect is within the bearing, and the approximate size of the defect. Laboratory testing is performed on the single bearing and four bearing test rigs housed at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV). The algorithm uses a four second sample window of the recorded vibration data and can reliably identify the defective component inside the bearing with up to a 100% confidence level. However, about 20,000 data points are used for this analysis, which requires substantial computational power. This can limit the battery life of the wireless onboard condition monitoring system. So, reducing the vibration sample window to conduct an accurate analysis should result in a more optimal power-efficient algorithm. A wireless onboard condition monitoring module that collects one second of vibration data (5,200 samples) was manufactured and tested to compare its efficacy against a wired setup that uses a four second sample window. This study investigates the root-mean-square values of the bearing vibration and its power spectral density plots to create an optimized and accurate algorithm for wireless utilization.​​​​

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Optimizing Power Consumption of Freight Railroad Bearings Using Laboratory Experimental Data

INTELLCONT_AUTH.INSTITUTION: University of Texas Rio Grande Valley

University of Texas Rio Grande Valley

INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT:
Based on projected freight truck fuel efficiency, freight railroad and equipment suppliers need to identify, evaluate and implement technologies and/or operating practices to maintain traditional railroad economic competitiveness. The railway industry uses systems that record the total energy efficiency of a train but not energy efficiency or consumption by components. Lowering the energy consumption of certain train components will result in an increase in its overall energy efficiency, which will yield cost benefits for all the stakeholders. One component of interest is the railroad bearing whose power consumption varies depending on several factors that include railcar load, train speed, condition of bearing whether it is healthy or defective, and type of defect. Being able to quantify the bearing power consumption, as a function of the variables mentioned earlier, would make it possible to obtain optimal operating condition ranges that minimize energy consumption and maximize train energy efficiency.
Several theoretical studies were performed to estimate the power consumption within railroad bearings, but those studies lacked experimental validation. For almost a decade now, the University Transportation Center for Railway Safety (UTCRS) at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) has been collecting power consumption data for railroad bearings under various loads, speeds, ambient temperatures, and bearing condition. The objective of this ongoing study is to use the experimentally acquired power consumption to come up with a correlation that can be used to quantify the bearing power consumption as a function of load, speed, ambient temperature, and bearing condition. Once obtained, the model can then be used to determine optimal operating practices that maximize the railroad bearing energy efficiency. In addition, the developed model will provide insight into possible areas of improvement for the next generation of energy efficient railroad bearings. This paper will discuss ongoing work including experimental setup and findings of energy consumption of bearings as function of railcar load, train speed, condition of bearing whether it is healthy or defective, and type of defect. Findings of energy consumption are converted into approximations of diesel gallons to quantify the effect of nominal energy consumption of the bearings and show economic value and environmental impact.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Onboard Load Sensor for Use in Freight Railcar Applications

INTELLCONT_AUTH.INSTITUTION: University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
University of Texas Rio Grande Valley

INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Approximately 40% of intercity freight transportation occurs by rail, making it the most widely used method of transporting large commodities. This trend is expected to persist over the next thirty years as our highway systems are strained and experiencing increased congestion and costly delays. Currently, the load of freight railcars is typically measured by weighbridges or retrofitted tracks at isolated locations. This practice is not efficient and limited by the fact that the load of the railcar cannot be monitored continuously, not to mention the inherent inaccuracies of such systems. Hence, there is great merit for an onboard load sensor that can accurately and effectively track the load of a railcar, minimizing overloading issues that can result in costly fines and damages to the rail infrastructure. The proposed onboard load sensor equipped with temperature sensing capability can also be used in bearing condition monitoring, as it will be able to identify unbalanced loading of the railcar. This paper provides proof of concept validation for an onboard railcar load sensor and presents analysis on the accuracy of two proposed correlations: one second-order model, and one multivariate model that incorporates the bearing operating temperature as read by the onboard sensor. The proposed load sensor can be readily implemented in freight railcars with minimal adjustments to the current bearing-adapter assembly. Laboratory testing is used to extrapolate different hypothetical operation scenarios that serve to demonstrate the use of this sensor in field service. The incorporation of the temperature sensors to the proposed onboard load sensing system provides added condition monitoring capability and allows for a much-improved load measurement with an accuracy of within 2% of the actual value.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Prognostics Models for Railroad Tapered Roller Bearings with Spall Defects on Inner or Outer Rings

University of Texas Rio Grande Valley

INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Rolling contact fatigue (RCF) is one of the major causes of failure in railroad bearings used in freight service. Subsurface inclusions resulting from impurities in the steel used to fabricate the bearings initiate subsurface fatigue cracks, which propagate upwards and cause spalling of the rolling surfaces. These spalls start small and propagate as continued operation induces additional crack formation and spalling. Studies have shown that the bearing temperature is not a good indicator of spall initiation. In many instances, the temperature of the bearing increases markedly only when the spall has spread across major portions of the raceway. In contrast, vibration signatures can be used to accurately detect spall initiation within a bearing and can track spall deterioration. No monitoring technique can indicate the growth rate of a spall or determine residual useful life. Hence, the main objective of this study is to develop reliable prognostic models for spall growth within railroad bearings that are based on actual service life testing rather than theoretical simulations. The data used to devise the models presented here were acquired from laboratory and field testing that started in 2010. Growth models are provided for spalls initiating on the bearing inner (cone) and outer (cup) rings. Coupling these prognostic models with a previously developed vibration-based bearing condition monitoring algorithm will provide the rail industry with an efficient tool that can be used to plan proactive maintenance schedules that will mitigate unnecessary and costly train stoppages and delays and will prevent catastrophic derailments.

INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Wayside hot-box detectors (HBDs) are devices used to assess the health of railcar components including bearings, axles, and brakes by monitoring their temperatures. HBDs use infrared (IR) sensors to record the temperatures of railroad bearings. Bearings that trigger an alarm or exhibit warm trending are removed and sent for inspection. In many cases, no discernable defects were found in the flagged bearings. Motivated by this finding, an investigation was conducted which included performing a controlled field test as well as exhaustive laboratory testing utilizing an HBD simulator. Data acquired from field and laboratory testing was used to evaluate the accuracy and efficacy of wayside HBDs. The results suggest that the scanning location on the bearing cup significantly affects the temperature measurement. Different calibrations for the field- and laboratory-acquired data were also explored. An optimized calibration technique along with proper IR sensor alignment can markedly improve the accuracy of HBD measurements.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: The Educational Value of Modelling Complex Thermodynamic Systems with System Dynamics Software
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: The solution of problems involving complex thermodynamic systems often occupies much of a students' time and can be a distraction from them developing a clear understanding of system components, interaction of subsystems, modelling simplifications and assumptions, and design optimization.  Refocusing students on the fundamental concepts of thermal systems design and analysis is possible with the introduction of system modelling software that carries some of the load of repetitive calculation required for complex systems.  Models of thermodynamic systems encountered in an advanced undergraduate thermodynamics course were developed by students (some provided to students) to solve homework problems of complex steam power plants, internal combustion engines, gas turbine power plants, refrigeration, and building energy systems.  Computer modelling systems used included two commercial modelling programs, an open source program, and systems developed by the authors.  Use of the modelling software forced students to setup problems in the same way as if solved on paper but allowed them to identify common components and processes that could be modeled by common blocks and used in multiple thermal systems.  One example presented is a simple process block that gives the state for any location in a converging/diverging supersonic nozzle with a normal shock.  The initial implementation has resulted in positive feedback from students and an improved self-efficacy in understanding and modelling complex thermodynamic systems not presented in class.

INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT:
The AdapterPlusTM steering pad is a polymer component on a railcar that helps to reduce stresses on the axle as a railcar rounds a curve. One railway application requires a minimum of 240 mA to be passed through the steering pad to the rail, which activates air valves that control automated cargo gates. Currently, two copper studs are inserted into the pad to provide a conductive path. However, after continuous cyclic loading caused by normal service operation, the copper studs deform, wear, and eventually lose contact between the two surfaces rendering the pad nonconductive. One proposed solution to this problem is to create a steering pad made entirely from an electrically conductive material. The University Transportation Center for Railway Safety (UTCRS) research team has successfully created a conductive nanocomposite made from vapor grown carbon nanofibers (CNFs) and a modified form of Elastollan 1195A thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU). Previous attempts to create this material were promising but failed to produce an electrically conductive specimen when injection molded. Preliminary results have shown that the new material can be injection molded to create an electrically conductive test specimen.
An injection molded insert was designed, fabricated, and incorporated into the existing steering pad design for further testing. Pressure measurement film had previously been used to find the points of maximum stress inside the pad to optimize the design of the composite insert. Characterization of the resistivity of the composite material was carried out in order to verify functionality in future iterations of this product. The resistance of the composite material is expected to be non-linear with a strong dependence on load and voltage. Conductivity tests were performed using a material testing system with a compressive load ranging from 1500 pounds to 5500 pounds. The voltage at each load was also varied between 10V to 20V and the non-linear resistance of the material was examined. The results have shown that the CNF/TPU composite is a potential replacement for the current TPU used for the pad and, with minimal modifications, can be implemented in field service operation.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Developing and Testing an Electronic Homework System to Improve Student Engagement and Learning in Engineering Thermodynamics
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: An electronic homework delivery system was developed for an advanced undergraduate engineering thermodynamics course due to limitations in available electronic homework systems. A commercially available system was effectively used in the introductory course for simple problems. The complexity of problems in the advanced course made adoption of the same system problematic as students needed feedback in the problem-solving process. A system was devised that delivers individual problems to each student, provides feedback throughout the process, and records results for assessment. The system has helped students become more active in homework assignments in both completing assignments and in doing original work. Over time, students would share general solutions from previous semesters and shortcut a deeper understanding of the problems. A recent addition to the system has been the introduction of problems that are based on fundamental concepts rather than using the right equation to get the correct numerical answer. A successful problem implementation gives students a randomly generated 4-6 state heat engine cycle (from 200 developed cycles) that does not correlate with any cycle in literature. Students are forced to work through the basic steps of evaluating a new process relying on their own understanding without being aided by a Google search or a classmate. The overall impact of the system along with the latest addition to student learning are presented.

(3) Workload Policies
• Organize the research in the college and formulate groups that fit within the major ongoing research initiatives such as Materials Science, Transportation, Renewable Energy, smart-energy systems, aerospace, thermal/fluid sciences, Biomechanical and Biomedical, Cyber Security and Information Systems, education, and others.
• Facilitate collaborations between the faculty in the college and encourage them to form productive research groups within the college and across other colleges and communicate effectively towards submitting proposals to federal and state agencies.

• Mentor the new tenure track faculty and provide them with guidelines that will help them establish realistic and productive expectations from themselves on their way to getting tenured and promoted.
• Work with the Dean to obtain professional staff and grant writers that can help faculty identify appropriate grant opportunities in their fields of expertise and assist them in writing these grants.

Assist the Dean in all matters related to the Graduate Programs which include working with all the department graduate program coordinators to increase recruitment, retention, and admission of students in the graduate programs and ensure that the graduate student affairs are taken care off.
